source_text: [FYTTE THE FIRST.] — Siþen þe sege & þe assaut wat3 sesed at Troye,
target_text: FYTTE THE FIRST — 1. After the siege and the assault had ceased at Troy, the city been destroyed and burned to brands and ashes, the warrior who wrought there the trains of treason was tried for his treachery, the truest on earth.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text:
Hit wat3 Ennias þe athel, & his highe kynde,
Þat siþen depreced prouinces, & patrounes bicome
Welne3e of al þe wele in þe west iles,
target_text: This was Aeneas the noble; he and his high kindred afterwards conquered provinces, and became patrons of well nigh all the wealth in the West Isles.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

target_text: As soon as rich Romulus turns him to Rome, with great pride he at once builds that city, and names it with his own name, which it now has; Ticius turns to Tuscany and founds dwellings; Longobard raises homes in Lombardy; and, far over the French flood, Felix Brutus establishes Britain joyfully on many broad banks, where war and waste and wonders by turns have since dwelt, and many a swift interchange of bliss and woe.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

target_text: And when this Britain was founded by this great hero, bold men loving strife bred therein, and many a time they wrought destruction.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text:
Mo ferlyes on þis folde han fallen here oft
Þen in any oþer þat I wot, syn þat ilk tyme.
Bot of alle þat here bult of Bretaygne kynges
Ay wat3 Arthur þe hendest; as I haf herde telle;
target_text: More strange things have happened in this land since these days than in any other that I know, but of all the British kings that built here, Arthur was ever the most courteous, as I have heard tell.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

target_text: Therefore, I mean to tell of an adventure in the world, which some count strange and extraordinary even among the wonders of Arthur.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text:
If 3e wyl lysten þis laye bot on littel quile,
I schal telle hit, as-tit, as I in toun herde,
with tonge;
As hit is stad & stoken,
In stori stif & stronge,
With lel letteres loken,
In londe so hat3 ben longe.
target_text: If ye will listen to this lay but a little while, I will tell it forthright as I heard it told in town, as it is set down in story that cannot be changed, long written in the land in true words.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text:
Þis kyng lay at Camylot vpon kryst-masse,
With mony luflych lorde, lede3 of þe best,
Rekenly of þe rounde table alle þo rich breþer,
With rych reuel ory3t, & rechles merþes;
target_text: This King lay royally at Camelot at Christmas tide with many fine lords, the best of men, all the rich brethren of the Round Table, with right rich revel and careless mirth.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: Þer tournayed tulkes bi-tyme3 ful mony,
target_text: There full many heroes tourneyed betimes,

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: Such glaumande gle glorious to here, Dere dyn vp-on day, daunsyng on ny3tes,
target_text: Such a merry tumult, glorious to hear; joyful din by day, dancing at night.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: Al wat3 hap vpon he3e in halle3 & chambre3, With lorde3 & ladies, as leuest him þo3t;
target_text: All was high joy in halls and chambers with lords and ladies as pleased them best.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: With all þe wele of þe worlde þay woned þer samen, Þe most kyd kny3te3 vnder kryste seluen, & þe louelokkest ladies þat euer lif haden, & he þe comlokest kyng þat þe court haldes;
target_text: With all the weal in the world they dwelt there together, the most famous knights save only Christ, the loveliest ladies that ever had life, and he, the comeliest of kings, who holds the court.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: For al wat3 þis fayre folk in her first age, on sille; Þe hapnest vnder heuen, Kyng hy3est mon of wylle,
target_text: For all this fair company were in their prime in the hall, the happiest troop under heaven with the proudest of kings.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: Hit were now gret nye to neuen So hardy a here on hille.
target_text: Truly it would be hard to name anywhere so brave a band.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: Wyle nw 3er wat3 so 3ep þat hit wat3 nwe cummen, Þat day doubble on þe dece wat3 þe douth serued,
target_text: When New Year was fresh and but newly come, the court was served double on the dais.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: Fro þe kyng wat3 cummen with kny3tes in to þe halle, Þe chauntre of þe chapel cheued to an ende; Loude crye wat3 þer kest of clerke3 & oþer,
target_text: As soon as the king with his knights was come into the hall, the chanting in the chapel came to an end; loud was the cry there of clerks and others.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: Nowel nayted o-newe, neuened ful ofte; & syþen riche forth runnen to reche honde-selle, 3e3ed 3eres 3iftes on hi3, 3elde hem bi hond, Debated busyly aboute þo giftes; Ladies la3ed ful loude, þo3 þay lost haden, & he þat wan wat3 not wrothe, þat may 3e wel trawe.
target_text: Noel was celebrated anew, shouted full often; and afterwards the great ones ran about to take handsel; called aloud for New Year’s gifts; ladies laughed full loud, though they had lost; and he that won was not wroth, that may ye well trow.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: Alle þis mirþe þay maden to þe mete tyme;
target_text: All this mirth they made till the meat time.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: When þay had waschen, worþyly þay wenten to sete, Þe best burne ay abof, as hit best semed;
target_text: When they had washed, worthily they went to their seats, the best man ever above, as it best behoved.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: Whene Guenore ful gay, grayþed in þe myddes. Dressed on þe dere des, dubbed al aboute,
target_text: Queen Guinevere full beauteous was set in the midst, placed on the rich dais adorned all about.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: Smal sendal bisides, a selure hir ouer Of tryed Tolouse, of Tars tapites in-noghe, Þat were enbrawded & beten wyth þe best gemmes, Þat my3t be preued of prys wyth penyes to bye,
target_text: Fine silk at the sides, a canopy over her of precious cloth of Toulouse and tapestries of Tars, that were embroidered and set with the best gems that money could buy.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: Þe comlokest to discrye, Þer glent with y3en gray, A semloker þat euer he sy3e, Soth mo3t no mon say.
target_text: Truly no man could say that he ever beheld a comelier lady than she, with her dancing gray eyes.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: V. — Bot Arthure wolde not ete til al were serued,
target_text: 5. But Arthur would not eat till all were served.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: He wat3 so Ioly of his Ioyfnes, & sum-quat child gered, His lif liked hym ly3t, he louied þe lasse Auþer to lenge lye, or to longe sitte, So bi-sied him his 3onge blod & his brayn wylde;
target_text: He was so merry in his mirth, and somewhat childlike in his manner; his life pleased him well; he loved little either to lie long or to sit long, so busied him his young blood and his wild brain.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: & also anoþer maner meued him eke, Þat he þur3 nobelay had nomen, ho wolde neuer ete Vpon such a dere day, er hym deuised were Of sum auenturus þyng an vncouþe tale, Of sum mayn meruayle, þat he my3t trawe, Of alderes, of armes, of oþer auenturus, Oþer sum segg hym bi-so3t of sum siker kny3t, To Ioyne wyth hym in iustyng in Iopardé to lay, Lede lif for lyf, leue vchon oþer, As fortune wolde fulsun hom þe fayrer to haue.
target_text: And another custom moved him also, that he through chivalry had taken up; he would never eat upon such a dear day before he was told an uncouth tale of some adventurous thing, of some great marvel that he could believe, of ancient heroes, of arms, or of other adventures; or unless some person demanded of him a sure knight to join with him in jousting, to incur peril, to risk life against life, trusting each in the other, leaving the victory to fortune.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: Þis wat3 [þe] kynges countenaunce where he in court were, At vch farand fest among his fre meny, in halle;
target_text: This was the king’s custom whenever he held court at each goodly feast among his

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: Thus þer stondes in stale þe stif kyng his-seluen, Talkkande bifore þe hy3e table of trifles ful hende
target_text: 6. Thus the great king stands waiting before the high table, talking of trifles full courteously.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: There gode Gawan wat3 grayþed, Gwenore bisyde & Agrauayn a la dure mayn on þat oþer syde sittes Boþe þe kynges sister sunes, & ful siker kni3tes;
target_text: The good Gawain was placed there beside Guinevere, and Agravain of the Hard Hand sat on the other side, both of them the king's sister's sons and full sure knights.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: Bischop Bawdewyn abof bi-gine3 þe table, & Ywan, Vryn son, ette wit hym-seluen;
target_text: Bishop Baldwin at the top begins the table, and Ywain, Urien's son, ate by himself.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: Þise were di3t on þe des, & derworþly serued, & siþen mony siker segge at þe sidborde3.
target_text: These were placed on the dais and honorably served, and after them many a good man at the side tables.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: Þen þe first cors come with crakkyng of trumpes, Wyth mony baner ful bry3t, þat þer-bi henged, Nwe nakryn noyse with þe noble pipes, Wylde werbles & wy3t wakned lote, Þat mony hert ful hi3e hef at her towches;
target_text: Then the first course came in with blare of trumpets, which were hung with many a bright banner. A new noise of kettle-drums with the noble pipes, wild and stirring melodies wakened the echoes; that many a heart heaved full high at their tones.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: Dayntes dryuen þer-wyth of ful dere metes, Foysoun of þe fresche, & on so fele disches, Þat pine to fynde þe place þe peple bi-forne For to sette þe syluener, þat sere sewes halden, on clothe;
target_text: Dainties of precious meats followed, foison of fresh viands, and on so many dishes that it was difficult to find place before the people to set on the cloth the silver that held the several courses.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: Iche lede as he loued hym-selue Þer laght with-outen loþe,
target_text: Each man as he himself preferred partook without hesitation.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: Ay two had disches twelue, Good ber, & bry3t wyn boþe.
target_text: Every two had twelve dishes between them, good beer and bright wine both.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: VII — Now wyl I of hor seruise say yow no more, For vch wyȝe may wel wit no wont þat þer were;
target_text: 7. Now will I tell you no more of their service, for everybody must well understand that there was no lack of opportunity for the people to take their food.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: An oþer noyse ful newe ne3ed biliue, Þat þe lude my3t haf leue lif-lode to cach. For vneþe wat3 þe noyce not a whyle sesed, & þe fyrst cource in þe court kyndely serued,
target_text: Another noise full new suddenly drew nigh, for scarcely had the music ceased a moment, and the first course been properly served in the court, than there burst in at the hall door an awesome being, in height one of the tallest men in the world;

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: Þer hales in at þe halle dor an aghlich mayster, On þe most on þe molde on mesure hyghe; Fro þe swyre to þe swange so sware & so þik,
target_text: than there burst in at the hall door an awesome being, in height one of the tallest men in the world; from the neck to the waist so square and so thick was he,

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: & his lyndes & his lymes so longe & so grete, Half etayn in erde I hope þat he were. Bot mon most I algate mynn hym to bene, & þat þe myriest in his muckel þat my3t ride;
target_text: and his loins and his limbs so long and so great, that half giant I believed him to have been, or, at any rate, the largest of men, and withal the handsomest in spite of his bulk, that ever rode;

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: For of bak & of brest al were his bodi sturne, Bot his wombe & his wast were worthily smale, & alle his fetures fol3ande, in forme þat he hade, ful clene;
target_text: for though his back and breast were so vast, yet his belly and waist were properly slim; and all his form according, full fairly shaped.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: For wonder of his hwe men hade, Set in his semblaunt sene; He ferde as freke were fade, & ouer-al enker grene.
target_text: At the hue of his noble face men wondered; he carried himself in hostile fashion and was entirely green.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: & his hod boþe, Þat wat3 la3t fro his lokke3, & layde on his schulderes Heme wel haled, hose of þat same grene,
target_text: and such his hood also, that was caught back from his locks and lay on his shoulders, the hem well stretched; hose of the same green, that clung to his calf;

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: Þat spenet on his sparlyr, & clene spures vnder, Of bry3t golde, vpon silk bordes, barred ful ryche & scholes vnder schankes, þere þe schalk rides;
target_text: and clean spurs under, of bright gold upon silk bands richly barred, and shoes on his shanks as the hero rides.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: & alle his vesture uerayly wat3 clene verdure, Boþe þe barres of his belt & oþer blyþe stones, Þat were richely rayled in his aray clene, Aboutte hym-self & his sadel, vpon silk werke3,
target_text: And all his vesture verily was clean verdure, both the bars of his belt, and the other beauteous stones that were set in fine array about himself and his saddle, worked on silk.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: Þat were to tor for to telle of tryfles þe halue, Þat were enbrauded abof, wyth bryddes & fly3es, With gay gaudi of grene, þe golde ay in myddes;
target_text: It would be too difficult to tell the half of the trifles that were embroidered there, with birds and flies, with gay gauds of green,—the good over in the middle;

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: Þe pendauntes of his payttrure, þe proude cropure His molaynes, & alle þe metail anamayld was þenne
target_text: the pendants of the poitrel, the proud crupper, the bits,—and all the metal was enamelled;

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: Þe steropes þat he stod on, stayned of þe same, & his arsoun3 al after, & his aþel sturtes, Þat euer glemered & glent al of grene stones.
target_text: the stirrups that he stood on were coloured the same, and his saddle bow likewise, and his fine reins that glimmered and glinted all of green stones.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: Þe fole þat he ferkkes on, fyn of þat ilke, sertayn; A grene hors gret & þikke, A stede ful stif to strayne, In brawden brydel quik, To þe gome he wat3 ful gayn.
target_text: The horse that he rode on was of the same colour too, a green horse, great and thick, a steed full stiff to guide, in gay embroidered bridle, and one right dear to his master.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: Wel gay wat3 þis gome gered in grene, & þe here of his hed of his hors swete;
target_text: 9. This hero was splendidly dressed in green; and the hair of his head matched that of his horse;

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: A much berd as a busk ouer his brest henges,
target_text: fair flowing locks enfolded his shoulders; a beard as big as a bush hung over his breast;

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text:
Þat wyth his hi3lich here, þat of his hed reches,
Wat3 euesed al vmbe-torne, a-bof his elbowes,
Þat half his armes þer vnder were halched in þe wyse
Of a kynge3 capados, þat closes his swyre.
target_text: and it, together with his splendid hair that reached from his head, was trimmed evenly all round above his elbows, so that half his arms were caught thereunder in the manner of a king's hood, that covers his neck.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text:
Þe tayl & his toppyng twynnen of a sute,
& bounden boþe wyth a bande of a bry3t grene,
Dubbed wyth ful dere stone3, as þe dok lasted,
Syþen þrawen wyth a þwong a þwarle knot alofte,
Þer mony belle3 ful bry3t of brende golde rungen.
target_text: The tail and the forelock were twined in the same way, and both bound with a band of bright green, set with full precious stones the whole length of the dock, and then tied up with a thong in a tight knot; where rang many bells full bright of burnished gold.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

target_text: Such a steed in the world, such a hero as rides him, was never beheld in that hall before that time.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text:
He loked as layt so ly3t,
So sayd al þat hym sy3e,
target_text: His glances were like bright lightning, so said all that saw him.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text:
Hit semed as no mon my3t,
Vnder his dyntte3 dry3e.
target_text: It seemed as if no man could endure under his blows.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text:
X. — Wheþer hade he no helme ne hawb[e]rgh nauþer,
Ne no pysan, ne no plate þat pented to armes,
Ne no schafte, ne no schelde, to schwne ne to smyte,
Bot in his on honde he hade a holyn bobbe,
Þat is grattest in grene, when greue3 ar bare,
& an ax in his oþer, a hoge & vn-mete,
A spetos sparþe to expoun in spelle quo-so my3t;
target_text: 10. He had neither helm nor hauberk, nor gorget, armour nor breastplate, nor shaft nor shield to guard or to smite; but in his one hand he had a holly twig, that is greenest when groves are bare, and an axe in his other, a huge and prodigious one, a weapon merciless almost beyond description;

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text:
Þe hede of an eln3erde þe large lenkþe hade,
Þe grayn al of grene stele & of golde hewen,

target_text: When the lord had learned that he had that hero, he laughed aloud, so dear it seemed to him; and all the men in the castle made much joy at appearing promptly in the presence of him who contains in his own person all worth and prowess and gracious traits, and is ever praised; above all the men in the world his renown is the greatest.

target_text: Each warrior said full softly to his companion—“Now shall we see courteous turns of behaviour, and the blameless forms of noble talking; what profit there is in speech may we learn without asking since we have taken that fine father of nurture.

source_text: Þenne la3ande quod þe lorde, "now leng þe by-houes, For I schal teche yow to þat terme bi þe tyme3 ende, Þe grene chapayle vpon grounde, greue yow no more; Bot 3e schal be in yowre bed, burne, at þyn ese, Quyle forth dayej, & ferk on pe fyrst of pe 3ere, & cum to þat merk at mydmorn, to make quat yow like3 in spenne;
target_text: Then laughing quoth the lord, "Now it behooves thee to stay; for I shall direct you to that spot by the time's end—the green chapel upon the ground. Grieve you no more; for ye shall be in your bed, sir, at thine ease some days yet, and set out on the first of the year and come to that place at mid-morn, to do what you like.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text:
Dowelle3 whyle new 3eres daye, & rys, & rayke3 þenne,
Mon schal yow sette in waye, Hit is not two myle henne.
target_text: Stay till New Year's day; and rise and go then. One shall set you on your way; it is not two miles hence.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text:
XXIII — Þenne wat3 Gawan ful glad, & gomenly he la3ed,--
"Now I þonk yow þryuandely þur3 alle oþer þynge, Now acheued is my chaunce, I schal at your wylle Dowelle, & elle3 do quat 3e demen."
target_text: 23. — Then was Gawain full glad, and merrily he laughed; “Now I thank you especially for this above all other things; now that my quest is achieved, I shall dwell at your will, and do whatever else ye decide.”

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: Þenne sesed hym þe syre, & set hym bysyde, Let þe ladie3 be fette, to lyke hem þe better;
target_text: Then the sire seized him and set him beside him, and let the ladies be fetched to please them the better.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: Þer wat3 seme solace by hem-self stille; Þe lorde let for luf lote3 so myry, As wy3 þat wolde of his wyte, ne wyst quat he my3t.
target_text: Fair entertainment they had quietly among themselves; the lord in his jovial, friendly demeanor behaved as a man out of his wits that knew not what he did.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: Þenne he carped to þe kny3t, criande loude, "3e han demed to do þe dede þat I bidde; Wyl 3e halde þis hes here at þys one3?"
target_text: Then he spake to the knight, crying loud, “Ye have agree to do the deed that I bid. Will ye hold this hest here at once?”

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: "3e sir, for-soþe," sayd þe segge trwe, "Whyl I byde in yowre bor3e, be bayn to 3ow[r]e hest."
target_text: “Yea, sir, forsooth,” said the true hero, “while I stay in your castle I shall be obedient to your hest.”

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: "For 3e haf trauayled," quod þe tulk, "towen fro ferre, & syþen waked me wyth, 3e arn not wel waryst, Nauþer of sostnaunce ne of slepe, soþly I knowe; 3e schal lenge in your lofte, & ly3e in your ese, To morn quyle þe messe-quyle, & to mete wende, When 3e wyl, wyth my wyf, þat wyth yow schal sitte, & comfort yow with compayny, til I to cort torne, 3e lende; & I schal erly ryse, On huntyng wyl I wende.
target_text: “Since ye have travelled from afar,” quoth the warrior, “and then have sat late with me, ye are not well nourished, I know, either with sustenance or with sleep. Ye shall linger in your loft and lie at your ease tomorrow till mass time; and go to meat when ye will with my wife, who shall sit with you and comfort you with her company till I return home; and I shall rise early and go hunting.”

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: Gauayn grante3 alle þyse, Hym heldande, as þe hende.
target_text: Gawain grants all this, bowing courteously.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: "3et firre," quod þe freke, "a forwarde we make; Quat-so-euer I wynne in þe wod, hit worþe3 to youre3, & quat chek so 3e acheue, chaunge me þer-forne; Swete, swap we so, sware with trawþe, Queþer, leude, so lymp lere oþer better."
target_text: 24. — “Yet further,” quoth the hero, “let us make an agreement. Whatsoever I win in the wood, it shall be yours; and whatsoever fortune ye achieve, exchange with me therefor. Sweet sir, swap we so, swear truly, whichever one of us gets the worse or the better.”

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: "Bi God," quod Gawayn þe gode, "I grant þer-tylle, & þat yow lyst forto layke, lef hit me þynkes."
target_text: “By God,” quoth Gawain the good, “I consent thereto; and whatever game you like, agreeable it seems to me.”

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: "Who bringe3 vus þis beuerage, þis bargayn is maked:" So sayde þe lorde of þat lede; þay la3ed vchone, Þay dronken, & daylyeden, & dalten vnty3tel, Þise lorde3 & ladye3, quyle þat hem lyked;
target_text: “On this beverage just brought the bargain is made,” said the lord of that people; and both laughed. Then they drank and played and amused themselves, these lords and ladies, so long as it pleased them;

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: & syþen with frenkysch fare & fele fayre lote3 Þay stoden, & stemed, & stylly speken, Kysten ful comlyly, & ka3ten her leue.
target_text: and then with polite demeanour and many fair gestures, they stood up and lingered a while, and talked quietly, kissed full comely, and took their leave.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: With mony leude ful ly3t, & lemande torches, Vche burne to his bed wat3 bro3t at þe laste, ful softe;
target_text: With many a gay servant and gleaming torches each hero was brought to his bed full softly at the last.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: To bed 3et er þay 3ede, Recorded couenaunte3 ofte; Þe olde lorde of þat leude, Cowþe wel halde layk a-lofte.
target_text: Yet before they went to bed they oft rehearsed the covenants. The old lord of that people knew well how to keep up a jest.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: FYTTE THE THIRD. I — Ful erly bifore þe day þe folk vp-rysen, Gestes þat go wolde, hor grome3 þay calden, & þay busken vp bilyue, blonkke3 to sadel, Tyffen he[r] takles, trussen her males, Richen hem þe rychest, to ryde alle arayde, Lepen vp ly3tly, lachen her brydeles, Vche wy3e on his way, þer hym wel lyked.
target_text: FYTTE THE THIRD 1. — Full early before the day the folk arose; the guests that would go called their grooms, and these hastened to saddle the horses, arrange their gear, and truss their mails. The great ones arrayed themselves to ride, leaped up lightly and caught their bridles, each wight on his way where it well pleased him.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: Þe leue lorde of þe londe wat3 not þe last, A-rayed for þe rydyng, with renkke3 ful mony; Ete a sop hastyly, when he hade herde masse, With bugle to bent felde he buske3 by-lyue; By þat þat any day-ly3t lemed vpon erþe, He with his haþeles on hy3e horsses weren.
target_text: The dear lord of the land was not the last; arrayed for the riding, with retainers full many, he ate a sop hastily after he had heard mass, and took his way quickly with his bugle to the field. By the time that any daylight gleamed upon the earth, he with his heroes were mounted on their high horses.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: Þenne þise cacheres þat couþe, cowpled hor hounde3, Vnclosed þe kenel dore, & calde hem þer-oute, Blwe bygly in bugle3 þre bare mote; Braches bayed þerfore, & breme noyse maked,
target_text: Then these hunters that understood it, coupled their hounds, unclosed the kennel doors and called them thereout, blew blithely on bugles three simple calls. At this the brachets bayed and made a wild noise,

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: & þay chastysed, & charred, on chasyng þat went; A hundreth of hunteres, as I haf herde telle, of þe best;
target_text: and the hunters chastised and turned back those that wandered off,—a hundred hunters of the best there were, as I have heard tell.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: Restayed with þe stablye, þat stoutly ascryed;
target_text: but quickly they were hindered by the beaters, who cried stoutly.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: Þay let þe hertte3 haf þe gate, with þe hy3e hedes, Þe breme bukke3 also, with hor brode paume3; For þe fre lorde hade de-fende in fermysoun tyme, Þat þer schulde no mon mene to þe male dere.
target_text: They let the harts with the high head go their way, the wild bucks also with their broad palms, for the generous lord had forbidden that there should any man meddle with the male deer in the close season.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: Þe hinde3 were halden in, with hay & war, Þe does dryuen with gret dyn to þe depe slade3;
target_text: But the hinds were held back with “Hay!” and “Ho!” and the does driven with great din to the deep glades.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: Þer my3t mon se, as þay slypte, slentyng of arwes, At vche þat wende vnder wande wapped a flone, Þat bigly bote on þe broun, with ful brode hede3,
target_text: There might one see as they ran the flight of arrows; at each turn under the boughs out flew a shaft, that savagely bit on the brown hide with full broad heads.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: What! þay brayen, & bleden, bi bonkke3 þay de3en.
target_text: How they leaped and bled and died by the banks!

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: & ay rachches in a res radly hem fol3es, Huntere3 wyth hy3e horne hasted hem after, Wyth such a crakkande kry, as klyffes haden brusten;
target_text: And ever the hounds with a rush eagerly followed them; hunters with shrill horn hastened after with such a resounding cry as if cliffs had cracked.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: What wylde so at-waped wy3es þat schotten, Wat3 al to-raced & rent, at þe resayt.
target_text: What game escaped the men who shot was all run down and torn at the stands.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: Bi þay were tened at þe hy3e, & taysed to þe wattre3, Þe lede3 were so lerned at þe lo3e trysteres, & þe gre-hounde3 so grete, þat geten hem bylyue, & hem to fylched, as fast as freke3 my3t loke, þer ry3t.
target_text: The deer were pestered at the heights, and worried at the waters; the people were so alert at the low stations, and the greyhounds so great, that got them quickly and pulled them down as fast as a man could see.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: Þe lorde for blys abloy Ful oft con launce & ly3t, & drof þat day wyth Ioy Thus to þe derk ny3t.
target_text: The lord, shouting for joy, shot and alighted full oft, and passed the day thus with joy till the dark night.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: III. — Þus layke3 þis lorde by lynde wode3 eue3, & G. þe god mon, in gay bed lyge3, Lurkke3 quyl þe day-ly3t lemed on þe wowes, Vnder couertour ful clere, cortyned aboute;
target_text: 3. — So this lord sports by the eaves of the linden wood, and Gawain the good man lies in his gay bed; reposes till the day light gleams on the walls, under the beautiful coverlets, curtained about.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: & as in slomeryng he slode, sle3ly he herde A littel dyn at his dor, & derfly vpon; & he heue3 vp his hed out of þe cloþes, A corner of þe cortyn he ca3t vp a lyttel, & wayte3 warly þider-warde, quat hit be my3t.
target_text: And as he fell into a doze, faintly he heard a little din at the door, then distinctly; and he heaved up his head out of the clothes, caught up a corner of his curtain a little, and watched warily in that direction to see what it might be.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: Hit wat3 þe ladi, loflyest to be-holde, Þat dro3 þe dor after hir ful dernly & stylle, & bo3ed to-warde þe bed;
target_text: It was the lady, loveliest to behold, who drew the door to after her right slyly and quietly, and turned toward the bed.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: & þe burne schamed. & layde hym doun lystyly, & let as he slepte.
target_text: The hero grew bashful and laid himself down cunningly and pretended that he slept.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: & ho stepped stilly. & stel to his bedde, Kest vp þe cortyn, & creped with-inne, & set hir ful softly on þe bed-syde,
target_text: And she stepped quietly, and stole to his bed, cast up the curtain, and crept within, and seated herself full softly on the bedside,

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: Þe lede lay lurked a ful longe quyle, Compast in his concience to quat þat cace my3t Mene oþer amount,
target_text: The man lay pretending a full great while, bothered in his conscience what this affair might mean or amount to.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: to meruayle hym þo3t;
target_text: Marvellous it seemed to him.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: Bot 3et he sayde in hym-self, "more semly hit were To aspye wyth my spelle [in] space quat ho wolde."
target_text: But yet he said to himself, “More seemly would it be to find out by asking what she would.”

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: þen he wakenede, & wroth, & to hir warde torned, & vn-louked his y3e-lydde3, & let as hym wondered, & sayned hym, as bi his sa3e þe sauer to worthe, with hande;
target_text: Then he waked, and stretched, and turned to her; unlocked his eyelids, and made believe he was amazed, and crossed himself with his hand, to be the safer for his prayer.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: Wyth chynne & cheke ful swete, Boþe quit & red in-blande, Ful lufly con ho lete, Wyth lyppe3 smal la3ande.
target_text: With chin and cheek full sweet, of mingled white and red, right lovely she looked, with her small laughing lips.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: IV. — "God moroun, sir Gawayn," sayde þat fayr lady,
target_text: 4. — “Good morrow, Sir Gawain!” said that fair lady.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: "3e ar a sleper vn-sly3e, þat mon may slyde hider; Now ar 3e tan astyt, bot true vus may schape, I schal bynde yow in your bedde, þat be 3e trayst:"
target_text: “Ye are a careless sleeper when one can enter thus. Now ye are certainly taken; unless we can make a truce I shall bind you in your bed, ye may be sure of that!”

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: Al la3ande þe lady lanced þo bourde3.
target_text: All laughing the lady shot those jests.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: "Goud moroun g[aye]," quod Gawayn þe blyþe,
target_text: “Good morrow, fair one,” quoth Gawain the blithe.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: "Me schal worþe at your wille, & þat me wel lyke3, For I 3elde me 3ederly, & 3e3e after grace, & þat is þe best, be my dome, for me by-houe3 nede;"
target_text: “I shall be at your disposal, and that pleases me well, for I yield me outright and pray for grace,—and that is the best course, I judge, for I am in straits.”

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: & þus he bourded a-3ayn with mony a blyþe la3ter.
target_text: And thus he returned the jests with many a blithe laugh.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: "Bot wolde 3e, lady louely, þen leue me grante, & de-prece your prysoun, & pray hym to ryse, I wolde bo3e of þis bed, & busk me better, I schulde keuer þe more comfort to karp yow wyth."
target_text: “But would ye, lovely lady, grant me leave, free your prisoner and bid him rise, I would leave this bed and dress myself better. Then I could talk with you in more comfort.”

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: "Nay, for soþe, beau sir," sayd þat swete, "3e schal not rise of your bedde, I rych yow better,
target_text: “Nay, forsooth, fair sir,” said that sweet one, “ye shall not rise from your bed; I shall manage you better.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: I schal happe yow here þat oþer half als, & syþen karp wyth my kny3t þat I ka3t haue; For I wene wel, Iwysse, sir Wawen 3e are, Þat alle þe worlde worchipe3, quere-so 3e ride;
target_text: I shall tie you up securely, and afterwards talk with my knight that I have caught; for I ween well, ye are indeed Sir Gawain, whom all the world worships whereso ye ride.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: Your honour, your hendelayk is hendely praysed
target_text: Your honour, your courtesy, is heartily praised

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: Bot hit ar ladyes in-no3e, þat leuer wer nowþe Haf þe hende in hor holde, as I þe habbe here, To daly witt derely your daynté worde3, Keuer hem comfort, & colen her care3, Þen much of þe garysourn oþer golde þat þay hauen; Bot I louue þat ilk lorde þat þe lyfte halde3, I haf hit holly in my honde þat al desyres, þur3e grace."
target_text: But there are ladies enough who were liefer have this courteous one in their power—as I have thee here,—to dally dearly with your dainty words, to comfort themselves and dispel their cares,—than much of the treasure and gold that they have. But I praise the Lord who rules the skies that through his grace I have wholly in my hand that which all desire.”

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: Scho made hym so gret chere, Þat wat3 so fayr of face, Þe kny3t with speches skere, A[n]swared to vche a cace.
target_text: Great cheer she that was so fair of face made him; the knight with discreet speeches answered her every proposal.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: VI. — "Madame," quod þe myry mon, "Mary yow 3elde, For I haf founden, in god fayth, yowre fraunchis nobele, & oþer ful much of oþer folk fongen hor dede3; Bot þe daynté þat þay delen for my disert nysen, Hit is þe worchyp of your-self, þat no3t hot wel conne3."
target_text: 6. — “Madame,” quoth the merry man, “Mary reward you, for in good faith I have found your generosity noble. People judge a person’s deeds largely from the accounts of others; but the praise that they accord my deserts is but idle. It is simply your own nobility, who know nothing but good.”

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: "Bi Mary," quod þe menskful, "me þynk hit anoþer; For were I worth al þe wone of wymmen alyue, & al þe wele of þe worlde were in my honde, & I schulde chepen & chose, to cheue me a lorde, For þe costes þat I haf knowen vpun þe kny3t here, Of bewté, & debonerté, & blyþe semblaunt, & þat I haf er herkkened, & halde hit here trwee, Þer schulde no freke vpon folde bifore yow be chosen."
target_text: “By Mary,” quoth the gracious one, “methinks it is otherwise; for were I worth all the store of women alive, and all the wealth of the world were in my hands, and I should bargain and choose to get me a “lord, then for the good traits that I have found in the knight here, of beauty and graciousness and gay seeming, and from what I have heard before and hold in this case to be true, there should no hero in the world be chosen before you.”

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: "I-wysse, worþy," quod þe wy3e, "3e haf waled wel better, Bot I am proude of þe prys þat 3e put on me, & soberly your seruaunt my souerayn I holde yow, & yowre kny3t I be-com, & Kryst yow for-3elde."
target_text: “Indeed, worthy one,” quoth the hero, “ye might have chosen much better; but I am proud of the estimation that ye put upon me; and as your devoted servant I hold you my sovereign, and your knight I become; and Christ pay you for it.”

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

target_text: Thus they spoke of various things till past the midmorn; and ever the lady behaved as if she loved him much.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

target_text: “Though I were the fairest of women,” mused the lady, “little love would he show, because of the danger that he seeks without reproach—the blow that may slay him, but must needs be undergone.”

target_text: 7. — Then she gave him good day, and of a sudden laughed; and as she stood there she astonished him with right sharp words; “Now may he that speeds each speech, pay you for this entertainment; but that ye are Gawain, it goes not in my mind.”

target_text: Never was a hero fairer entertained by two such worthy dames, the other and the younger. Much disport they make together.

source_text: Ho commes to þe cortyn, & at þe kny3t totes, Sir Wawen her welcumed worþy on fyrst, & ho hym 3elde3 a3ayn, ful 3erne of hir worde3, Sette3 hir softly by his syde, & swyþely ho la3e3, & wyth a luflych loke ho layde hym þyse worde3:
target_text: Sir Gawain at once welcomes her worthily, and she returns his greeting right promptly, seats herself softly by his side, laughs opens, and with a lovely look addresses these words to him:

source.author: Richard Morris

target_text: “Sir, if ye be Gawain, it seems to me a very strange thing that a man of such quality should not follow the conventions of good society; and should after making acquaintance with a person cast him utterly from his mind.

source.author: Richard Morris

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

target_text: “What is that?” quoth the hero. “Forsooth I know not. If what ye say be true, I am to blame.”

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

target_text: “Yet I taught you about kissing,” replied the fair lady; “wherever a countenance is known, quickly to claim a kiss; that becomes every knight who practices courtesy.”

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: "Do way," quod þat derf mon, "my dere, þat speche, For þat durst I not do, lest I denayed were, If I were werned, I were wrang I-wysse, 3if I profered."
target_text: “Cease such speech, my dear lady,” said the ready man. “I durst not claim it lest I should be denied. If I proposed and were refused, I should certainly be wrong in proffering.”

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: "Ma fay," quod þe mere wyf, "3e may not be werned, 3e ar stif in-noghe to constrayne wyth strenkþe, 3if yow lyke3, 3if any were so vilanous þat yow denaye wolde."
target_text: “By my faith,” quoth the lovely dame, “ye cannot be refused. Ye are strong enough to compel it by strength if ye pleased, supposing any were so ill-bred as to deny you.”

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

target_text: “Yea, by God,” said Gawain, “your speech is good; but violence is considered discourteous among my people, as is any gift that is not given with a good will.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: "I woled wyt at yow, wy3e," þat worþy þer sayde, & yow wrathed not þer-wyth, what were þe skylle, Þat so 3ong & so 3epe, as 3e ar at þis tyme, So cortayse, so kny3tyly, as 3e ar knowen oute, & of alle cheualry to chose, þe chef þyng a-losed, Is þe lel layk of luf, þe lettrure of armes;
target_text: “I should like to know from you, sir,” said the peerless lady, “if it vexes you not,—what might be the reason that so young and so gallant person as ye now are, one so courteous and so knightly as ye are known everywhere to be, have never spoken of love.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

source_text: For to telle of þis tenelyng of þis trwe kny3te3, Hit is þe tytelet, token, & tyxt of her werkke3, How ledes for her lele luf hor lyue3 han auntered, Endured for her drury dulful stounde3, & after wenged with her walour & voyded her care, & bro3t blysse in-to boure, with bountees hor awen.
target_text: For in relating the pains of true knights, the chief thing praised in all of chivalry is the royal sport of love,—and the science of arms: it is the title, token, and text of their works; how heroes for their true love adventured their lives, endured for their sweethearts doleful hours, and afterwards avenged themselves by their valour; dispersed their care, and brought bliss to bower, with plenteous rewards for themselves.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

target_text: And ye are the most renowned knight of your time; your fame and your worship walks everywhere,—and now I have sat by you here two separate times, yet have I never heard from your head a single word that pertained at all to love, less or more.

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight

target_text: And ye, that are so courteous and so distinguished in your vows, ought willingly to show and teach to a young thing some tokens of the art of true love.

target_text: But to take upon myself the task of expounding true love, of touching upon the themes of that text, and tales of arms before you, who I wot well have more knowledge of that sort by the half than I or a hundred such have, or ever shall have so long as I live,—that were a manifold folly by my troth, dear one.

target_text: Thus the fair lady besought him, and tried him oft, for to have won him to wrong,—whatever it was she purposed; but he defended himself fairly that no fault appeared, nor any evil on either side; they knew nought but joy. target_text: unless indeed ye have a sweetheart, a dearer being, that pleases you better, and ye have plighted faith so firmly to that gentle one that ye care not to loosen it.—Verily now that is what I believe,

source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

target_text: Kiss me now comely and I shall go hence. I can only mourn in the world as a maid that loved much.”

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

target_text: “Now, dear, at this departing do me this comfort; give me somewhat of thy gift, thy glove if it might be, that I may think on thee, sir, to lessen my mourning.”

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

target_text: “Now in truth,” quoth that man, “I would I had here for thy love, the dearest thing that I wield;

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
target.author: w A Neilson

target_text: and I am here on an errand in lands uncouth, and have no men with mails full of precious things for remembrance at this moment;

source.author: Richard Morris

target_text: “Now, courteous and honourable one,” quoth that lovesome lady, “though I shall have nothing of yours, yet shall ye have of mine.”

target_text: But the man refused it, and readily he said: “I desire no great gifts, my gay one, at this time. I have naught to give you, and naught will I take.”

source.work: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight
source.author: Richard Morris

target_text: And she sorrowed that he refused, and said thereafter, “If ye refuse my ring, since it seems too rich, and ye would not be so highly beholden to me, I shall give you my girdle, that will enrich you less.”

target_text: And therefore, I pray you, be not displeased, and give over your attempt; for I intend never to consent. I am dearly beholden to you because of your entertainment; and ever in hot and in cold I will be your true servant.

source.author: Richard Morris

A bende, a belef hym aboute, of a bry3t grene,
& þat, for sake of þat segge, in swete to were.
target_text: They laugh loud at his tale, and lovingly agree that the lords and the ladies that belong to the Table, each knight of the brotherhood, should have a baldric, an oblique band about him of a bright green, and wear that for the sake of the hero.

target_text: After Brutus the bold hero first came hither, when the siege and the assault had ceased at Troy, many adventures of this sort happened.
